claims.text: A random multi-element distribution in refractory high-entropy alloys produces severe lattice distortion.
Severe lattice distortion produces wavy, distorted edge-dislocation cores.
Wavy edge-dislocation cores impede dislocation mobility at high temperature.
The resulting dislocation mobility governs the extent of high-temperature plastic strain.
The resulting dislocation mobility governs high-temperature toughness.
The initial material is a BCC refractory high-entropy alloy of the NbTaTiV type.
The initial alloy has a homogeneous random elemental distribution.
The initial alloy contains minimal extrinsic impurities.
Two alloys can be kept identical in overall composition and processing while being made different in atomic size mismatch by substituting elements.
Substitution with elements of larger or smaller atomic radius will intentionally vary lattice distortion.
Testing at 700–900°C using controlled-rate mechanical loading and in situ diffraction is suitable for examining this NbTaTiV-type system.
Edge-dislocation cores deviate from their neutral or ideal slip planes because of lattice distortion.
Higher atomic size mismatch produces greater lattice distortion.
Reduced dislocation mobility at elevated temperature increases yield strength.
Reduced dislocation mobility limits plastic deformation and improves toughness.
Relative to the low-mismatch baseline, the high-mismatch alloys will have higher high-temperature yield strength.
Relative to the low-mismatch baseline, the high-mismatch alloys will exhibit less plastic strain.
Reduced plastic strain in the high-mismatch alloys is indicative of improved toughness.
Lower atomic size mismatch is expected to produce lower lattice distortion, higher dislocation mobility, lower yield strength, and lower high-temperature toughness.
The proposed scope is single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloys undergoing uniaxial deformation at 700–900°C.

contradictions.description: The intervention requires the comparison alloys to have identical overall composition while also changing one or more constituent elements by substitution. Elemental substitution changes composition and introduces chemical effects, so the stated comparison does not cleanly isolate atomic size mismatch.

The hypothesis treats reduced plastic strain as evidence of improved toughness without specifying fracture resistance or absorbed energy. Reduced strain and improved toughness are distinct outcomes, so the asserted identification is not internally justified.
